Spirituality of God
spir-i-choo-AL-i-tee of GOD
noun phrase (theology proper / divine attributes)
The divine attribute by which God is spirit — an immaterial, non-corporeal being, without body, parts, or physical extension. Grounded in Christ's words to the Samaritan woman (John 4:24, God is a Spirit) and the second-commandment prohibition of images. Westminster Confession II.1 (God is a most pure spirit... without body, parts, or passions).

Biblical Definition

The divine attribute by which God is spirit — an immaterial, non-corporeal being, without body, parts, or physical extension. The foundational text is the Lord Jesus's declaration to the Samaritan woman: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:24). God's spirituality means He has no physical body and is not composed of material parts; He is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17, the King eternal, immortal, invisible), not localized in space as bodies are, and not perceptible by the physical senses. The Westminster Confession (II.1) describes God as a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions. The biblical anthropomorphisms (references to God's hand, arm, eyes, face, etc.) are figures of speech accommodating divine truth to human understanding, not literal descriptions of a divine body; God is spirit. The second-commandment prohibition of images (Exodus 20:4-6) is grounded in God's spirituality: because God is spirit, He cannot and must not be represented by any material image; every attempt to make a visible image of the invisible God falsifies His spiritual nature and constitutes idolatry. The incarnation is the unique exception that proves the rule: in the incarnation, the eternal Son (who as God is spirit) took to Himself a true human body and nature, becoming visible and tangible (1 John 1:1-3); but this does not make the divine nature corporeal; the divine nature remains spirit, and the human nature of Christ is the visible, tangible humanity He assumed. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's spirituality against the anthropomorphite error (which attributes a literal body to God), the idolatrous image-making (which the second commandment forbids), and the materialist denial (which reduces all reality to matter). God is spirit; He must be worshiped in spirit and in truth; He cannot be represented by any material image; and the worship that pleases Him is spiritual worship grounded in truth, not the image-worship and sensory religion that violates His spiritual nature.

Webster 1828 Definition

The divine attribute by which God is spirit — immaterial, non-corporeal, without body, parts, or physical extension; John 4:24 (God is a Spirit); 1 Timothy 1:17 (invisible); Westminster II.1 (a most pure spirit); grounds the second-commandment prohibition of images.

SPIRITUALITY OF GOD, n. phr. (theology proper / divine attributes) God is spirit — immaterial, non-corporeal, without body, parts, or physical extension. Foundation: John 4:24 (God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth); 1 Timothy 1:17 (the King eternal, immortal, invisible); Westminster II.1 (a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions). The biblical anthropomorphisms (God's hand, arm, eyes, face) are accommodating figures of speech, not a literal divine body. The second-commandment prohibition of images (Exodus 20:4-6) is grounded in God's spirituality. The incarnation is the unique exception: the eternal Son took a true human body without making the divine nature corporeal. Held against anthropomorphite error, idolatrous image-making, and materialist denial.

Key Scripture

John 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

1 Timothy 1:17 — "Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen."

Exodus 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth."

Luke 24:39 — "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have."

Modern Corruption

The spirituality of God is held against the anthropomorphite error (a literal divine body), idolatrous image-making (forbidden by the second commandment), and materialist denial (reducing reality to matter); God is spirit and must be worshiped in spirit and truth.

The spirituality of God is held against several errors. The anthropomorphite error attributes a literal physical body to God, reading the biblical anthropomorphisms (God's hand, arm, eyes, face) as literal descriptions of a divine body; this contradicts the explicit teaching that God is spirit (John 4:24) and invisible (1 Timothy 1:17). The idolatrous image-making attempts to represent God by material images; this is forbidden by the second commandment precisely because God is spirit and cannot be truly represented by any material likeness (every image of God falsifies His spiritual nature and constitutes idolatry). The materialist denial reduces all reality to matter, denying the existence of spirit altogether. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God is spirit — immaterial, non-corporeal, invisible, without body or parts; He must be worshiped in spirit and in truth (John 4:24); He cannot and must not be represented by any material image (the second-commandment ground); the worship that pleases Him is spiritual worship grounded in His revealed truth, not image-worship and sensory religion. The substantive implication for worship is significant: the regulative principle of worship, the rejection of images in worship, and the centrality of the Word (the means by which the invisible spiritual God reveals Himself) all flow from the spirituality of God. The believer worships the invisible, spiritual God in spirit and in truth, through the Word and the appointed spiritual means, not through images and sensory religion that violate God's spiritual nature.

Hebrew Roots

John 4:24; 1 Timothy 1:17; Westminster II.1; God immaterial, non-corporeal, invisible, without body or parts; grounds the second-commandment prohibition of images; held against anthropomorphite, idolatrous, and materialist errors.
